title: A long-distance quantum repeater network

concept.text: A long-distance quantum repeater network would distribute usable entanglement among distant quantum devices through intermediate nodes. Entanglement is a shared quantum resource that, together with suitable local operations and classical communication, can support transferring quantum states between devices. The innovation is an integrated network that maintains this capability across multiple links and repeaters, with performance sufficient for an actual application.

Photons traveling through optical fiber are progressively lost, making direct entanglement distribution increasingly difficult as distance grows. Repeaters would establish entanglement over shorter segments, retain successful connections in quantum memories, and join them through entanglement swapping. Purification or other error-management methods would preserve the quality of the resulting connection. Classical control would coordinate generation, storage, measurements, and confirmation across the network. Unlike ordinary signal amplification, this process must respect the quantum-mechanical prohibition on copying an arbitrary unknown quantum state.

significance.text: Reliable entanglement distribution would give distant devices a shared quantum resource beyond classical message exchange. A useful network could make quantum-state transfer available across locations, allowing quantum systems to cooperate without placing every component in one facility. This is the central prospective advance; the cited experiment establishes a relevant component capability rather than these network-level benefits.

Possible downstream applications include distributed quantum sensing and connections between quantum processors. Their value would depend on the end devices, protocols, entanglement quality, delivery rate, and operating costs. A communication link alone does not establish an advantage in sensing or computation, and connecting processors does not automatically produce scalable distributed quantum computing.

Entanglement would not enable faster-than-light communication: quantum-state-transfer protocols still require classical communication. Nor would the network automatically secure every message. The supplied supplementary material retains requirements such as authenticated classical channels and reliable key management. Security would have to be established for the particular protocol and implementation, including any information disclosed during testing.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target capability is sustained delivery of useful end-to-end entanglement across an integrated, long-distance network containing multiple repeaters. Its components must work together as distance and node count increase: memories must preserve states while other links are established, photonic interfaces must generate entanglement efficiently, swapping must connect segments successfully, and error management must prevent accumulated imperfections from making the final state unusable. A successful isolated link does not establish this combined capability.

A concrete barrier is the relationship between probabilistic generation and memory lifetime. A stored connection can decay while the network waits for another segment to succeed. Increasing memory lifetime therefore helps only alongside adequate generation rates, state fidelity, and reliable swapping. Synchronization is another integration requirement: the reviewed supplement describes a handshake protocol aligning Alice, Bob, and the intervening station Charlie before heralded entanglement generation. Extending coordinated operation beyond a shared laboratory requires engineering that the reported laboratory result does not demonstrate.

Practical operation also requires complete application protocols and their supporting infrastructure. For device-independent quantum key distribution, producing entanglement is only part of the task: security analysis, authenticated classical communication, key management, and the implementation steps omitted from the laboratory demonstration must also be addressed. The supplied supplement explicitly leaves a complete practical field implementation to future work. This establishes a limitation of that experiment, without establishing the state of every other research effort.

current_state.text: On 2 February 2026, Wen-Zhao Liu and colleagues reported long-lived entanglement between ion memories connected through 10 km of spooled optical fiber. The reviewed revised supplement gives an entangled-state fidelity above 0.5 for 547 ± 34 milliseconds, compared with an average entanglement-generation time of approximately 450 milliseconds. It also reports an average fidelity of 0.578 ± 0.006 under an unbounded-wait procedure. These measurements support the specific achievement that entanglement survived longer than the average time needed to establish it, an important repeater building block.

The memory nodes were three meters apart in one laboratory and shared a master laser. The fiber lengths therefore describe the optical transmission paths, not geographic separation between independently operated facilities. The experiment demonstrates a two-memory link under laboratory conditions; it does not demonstrate a deployed network with multiple repeaters or multiple users.

The authors reported proof-of-principle device-independent quantum key distribution with finite-size analysis at 10 km, and a positive key rate at 101 km in the asymptotic limit. The 101 km claim is consequently an asymptotic key-rate result, not an established finite-data operational key service at that distance. The supplement also identifies omitted steps needed for a complete practical implementation.

The security interpretation remains qualified by the supplied peer-review record. A later reviewer questioned whether the analysis adequately accounted for information leakage from disclosed test outcomes. The authors defended their analysis, but the retained record does not resolve the disagreement. This supports attributing the key-distribution claims to the authors rather than treating practical device-independent security as conclusively established. Earlier lifetime objections concerned superseded measurements and do not contradict the revised lifetime values above.

These details are drawn from the supplied review: it had a publisher abstract and subscription preview rather than the full main article, a complete retained supplement with some garbled figure-label extraction, and a peer-review extraction that truncates on page 34. The relevant quantitative prose was readable, but no later resolution of the security dispute can be inferred from the truncated record. The supplied search record is empty, so the evidence does not establish the latest worldwide achievement or whether the broader network goal remained unmet on 1 November 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: operate a multi-repeater, multi-user network over deployed long-distance fiber and verify end-to-end entanglement delivered through successive swapping operations. Specify the distance, topology, users, observation period, and acceptance thresholds before testing. Set sustained delivery rate, fidelity, and availability requirements according to a stated application. These are proposed evaluation choices, not established standards prescribed by the supplied sources.
completion_criteria.label: Multi-repeater entanglement over deployed long-distance fiber meets application service requirements

completion_criteria.text: Proposed performance comparison: measure rate versus distance against a credible direct-transmission benchmark with explicitly comparable resources. State the assumptions and resource accounting used for each system, including the relevant memories, optical channels, hardware, and operating conditions. Report both successful delivery and interruptions over the observation period so that occasional high-quality events cannot stand in for sustained service.
completion_criteria.label: Rate versus distance compared against direct transmission with resource accounting

completion_criteria.text: Proposed utility and reproducibility test: use the delivered entanglement in a meaningful protocol and reproduce the result independently, with enough methodological and operating detail to assess the claimed performance. A security application should include the complete implementation and an analysis addressing disclosed test information and other protocol assumptions. A sensing or computing application should demonstrate its own stated benefit rather than infer it from entanglement delivery alone.
completion_criteria.label: Application benefit from delivered entanglement is independently reproduced

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: report the tested operating conditions, scaling limits, maintenance requirements, and conditions under which useful service fails. Tests across multiple distances, users, and configurations would establish demonstrated breadth within those conditions. Finite demonstrations would not establish operation at arbitrary distances, with unlimited users, or across every application.
completion_criteria.label: Tested operating boundaries and useful service failure conditions reported

related_concepts.text: Roster comparison and synthesis: ELE-02, “Fault-tolerant quantum computer with useful, scalable logical computation,” is the closest application-level neighbor. A repeater network could connect quantum processors, but useful logical computation and reliable inter-node entanglement are distinct achievements. Neither concept establishes the other, and a network could serve communication or sensing without connecting full fault-tolerant computers.

Roster comparison and synthesis: ELE-11, “Integrated photonic-electronic computing with broad system advantage,” overlaps in optical interfaces, control electronics, and system integration. Its target is computing advantage within a photonic-electronic system; ELE-03 targets distribution of quantum entanglement across locations. Optical hardware overlap does not make ordinary photonic computation equivalent to quantum networking.

Roster comparison and synthesis: ELE-10, “Broadly deployable, maintenance-free ambient-powered sensing,” shares a potential sensing context but addresses power supply, deployment, and maintenance. Entanglement-assisted distributed sensing would require suitable quantum sensors and protocols; it would not by itself supply ambient power or eliminate maintenance. ELE-09, “Resilient, self-restoring power networks,” shares concerns about network availability and recovery, while distributing electrical power rather than quantum states.

Roster comparison and synthesis: ELE-04, “Practical, energy-recovering reversible computing,” and ELE-08, “Manufacturable ultra-low-voltage switching for general-purpose electronics,” concern different approaches to electronic computation and energy use. They could affect supporting hardware but do not solve quantum-state storage or entanglement swapping. The remaining entries—ELE-01 superconducting conductors, ELE-05 long-duration electrical storage, ELE-06 two-way neural interfaces, and ELE-07 wireless electrical power delivery—have no direct enabling relationship established by the supplied evidence. Their goals remain distinct from a long-distance quantum repeater network.

The peer-review extraction ends on page 34; any subsequent resolution of the security disagreement is unknown.
The evidence does not establish the latest worldwide network achievement or whether the broader goal remained unmet on 1 November 2026.

brief.title: Quantum links between distant devices
possible: Quantum devices in different locations could transfer quantum states, the information they hold, through a long-distance network. They would share entanglement, a quantum connection that enables this transfer alongside ordinary messages.
why: Researchers could connect quantum processors and let quantum systems cooperate without gathering every component in one facility. Shared connections could also support sensing across distant locations.

sources.showed: They connected devices that store quantum states through 10 km of coiled fiber. Their entanglement survived longer than the average time needed to create it.
sources.quote: Here we demonstrate memory–memory entanglement between two nodes connected by 10 km of spooled fibre surviving beyond the average entanglement establishment time.
sources.cited_for: Stored connections can last long enough to wait while another connection is established.
sources.not_established: The devices shared a laboratory; the experiment did not demonstrate a long-distance network containing multiple repeaters.

sources.showed: They created entanglement between independent devices across a city. Any pair could share a connection, and the stored states lasted longer than a message's round trip.
sources.quote:
We demonstrate concurrent entanglement generation between any two
memory nodes.
sources.cited_for: Independent devices can establish and store quantum connections across a metropolitan network.
sources.not_established: The network did not join successive links through multiple repeaters to deliver long-distance service.

sources.showed: They used stored quantum states to join a pair of short links on demand. Storage improved how the connection rate changed as individual links became harder to establish.
sources.quote:
With the memory enhancement, scaling-changing acceleration is demonstrated in the rate for a
successful entanglement connection.
sources.cited_for: Quantum storage can improve the efficiency of joining links.
sources.not_established: This laboratory experiment did not demonstrate sustained service through a long-distance chain of repeaters.

sources.who: S. L. N. Hermans and colleagues at QuTech
sources.showed: They transferred a quantum state between devices without a direct link, using an intermediate device. The transfer was more faithful than the classical benchmark.
sources.quote:
Here we realize quantum teleportation between remote, non-neighbouring nodes in a
quantum network.
sources.cited_for: Joined links and stored entanglement can support quantum-state transfer through an intermediate device.
sources.not_established: The result did not establish useful application performance across a deployed long-distance network.

sources.who: Alexander N. Craddock and colleagues at Qunnect, NYU and Cisco Quantum Labs
sources.showed: In a preprint, they reported joining quantum connections over 17.6 km of deployed New York City fiber. The sources operated without shared lasers or optical frequency references.
sources.quote:
Using this layout, we achieve the
first Hz-level polarization entanglement swapping over a
commercially deployed network.
sources.cited_for: Quantum links from independent sources can be joined over deployed city fiber.
sources.not_established: Joining photon connections did not establish a network that stores states and delivers useful service through multiple repeaters.

shown: Wen-Zhao Liu and colleagues demonstrated storage that outlasted the average connection-making time, but their devices occupied one laboratory. Jian-Long Liu and colleagues demonstrated independent devices sharing entanglement across a city. These are separate parts of the capability.
missing: A deployed long-distance network must sustain useful entanglement through multiple repeaters, intermediate stations that store and join shorter links.
Storage, connection generation and error control must work together as more links and users join the network.
A complete application must demonstrate a benefit from the delivered connections, with its required supporting infrastructure.

milestones.label: Sustained useful connections through multiple repeaters
milestones.explanation: A deployed long-distance network serving multiple users would have to meet application requirements for connection quality, delivery rate and availability. This would establish that successive links work together.

milestones.label: Performance measured against direct transmission
milestones.explanation: Delivery rates across distances would have to be compared with direct transmission using comparable resources, including interruptions. This would reveal what repeaters deliver for the resources they consume.

milestones.label: An independently reproduced application benefit
milestones.explanation: An application using the delivered entanglement would have to show a meaningful benefit that another team reproduces. This would establish useful performance beyond creating a connection.

milestones.label: Known operating limits and failure conditions
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to establish operating limits, maintenance needs and when useful service fails across distances, users and configurations. This would define the conditions under which the network works.

uncertain: The connection quality, delivery rate and availability needed for each application remain to be defined, along with fair comparison rules.
It remains unclear how the demonstrated components perform together across multiple repeaters on deployed fiber.
Whether disclosed test outcomes leak information that undermines the claimed security of Liu and colleagues' key-sharing demonstration remains disputed.

page.title: Quantum repeater networks
page.definition: A fiber network distributes entanglement, joint quantum states that cannot be written as mixtures of separate states at each node, across continental distances. Cascaded quantum repeaters store and join shorter entangled links while correcting photon loss and operational errors.

goal.need: At 0.2 dB/km attenuation, an ideal pure-loss fiber transmits 1% of photons over 100 km and one in ten billion over 500 km. Its repeaterless entanglement-distribution capacity is −log₂(1−η) ebits per optical mode, where η is transmissivity and one ebit is a maximally entangled qubit pair. Repeaters address this exponential rate–distance limitation.

figures.caption: Calculated ideal repeaterless capacities for fiber attenuation of 0.2 dB/km.
figures.note: Calculated using η = 10^(−0.02L) and capacity −log₂(1−η), with L in kilometres. These asymptotic capacities permit unlimited two-way classical communication.

statements.body: National Institute of Standards and Technology
statements.quote: Ideally, quantum nodes at very large distances and possibly across the world need to be connected.

statements.body: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada
statements.quote: surpassing the fundamental limits of direct quantum transmission through a chosen channel.
statements.context: The Innovative Solutions Canada challenge opened on 21 May 2026 identifies this as the ultimate objective of networks supported by quantum repeater nodes.

completion.title: Cascaded quantum repeaters distribute error-corrected entanglement across continental distances.
completion.criterion: Distribute end-to-end entanglement over continental-scale distances through concatenated quantum repeaters. Classical and quantum networking operate together, and quantum communication corrects both loss and operational errors.
completion.set_by: US Department of Energy, Quantum Internet Blueprint, milestone 4.
completion.threshold_quote: quantum error corrected communication with respect to loss and operational errors over continental-scale distances
completion.basis: DOE places this capability after its intercity quantum memory-network stage. It tests integrated repeater concatenation and error correction across a continent. The source provides no numerical distance, rate, fidelity, availability or observation-period cutoff.

milestones.title: A Bell-state measurement connects entanglement across two repeater links.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate a Bell-state measurement, or an equivalent entanglement-swapping operation, enabling link-to-link entanglement distribution. Pu et al. (2021) connected two segments using two atomic memories. With each segment's preparation probability set to 0.1%, output Bell-state fidelity was 79.5 ± 4.8%, from 656 four-photon coincidences collected over 16 hours. The experiment also demonstrated approximately linear, rather than quadratic, connection-efficiency scaling with individual-link preparation probability.
milestones.set_by: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada, 2026 quantum-repeater challenge, mandatory entanglement-swapping outcome. This milestone uses its experimental demonstration option; the programme also accepts plans or models.

milestones.title: An elementary quantum link generates entanglement faster than its stored entanglement decays.
milestones.criterion: The entanglement-generation rate r_ent exceeds the stored-entanglement decoherence rate r_dec: η_link = r_ent/r_dec > 1. Liu et al. (2026) reported r_ent = 2.226 s⁻¹ and an entangled-state decay time of 550 ± 36 ms, giving η_link ≈ 1.2. Bell-state fidelity remained above 0.5 for 547 ± 34 ms, exceeding the approximately 450 ms mean generation time. The two ion memories were 3 m apart, shared a master laser, and were connected through 10 km of spooled fiber.
milestones.set_by: The quantum-link-efficiency benchmark used by Humphreys et al. in Nature (2018) and subsequently applied by Liu et al.
milestones.threshold_quote: Moving beyond current two-node networks requires the rate of entanglement generation between nodes to exceed their decoherence rates.

milestones.title: Qubits teleport between non-neighbouring nodes with average fidelity above 2/3.
milestones.criterion: Teleport the six equally weighted cardinal qubit states (±X, ±Y, ±Z) between non-neighbouring nodes, with average output-state fidelity above the classical measure-and-prepare bound of 2/3. Hermans et al., published on 25 May 2022, obtained 0.702 ± 0.011 at one teleportation per 117 s in a three-node diamond-spin network. These values describe their conditional teleportation protocol.
milestones.set_by: The classical qubit-teleportation benchmark applied by Hermans et al., Nature (2022).

milestones.title: Any two users in an intra-city network can obtain entanglement.
milestones.criterion: Any two users obtain entangled states, deterministically or heralded, and measure them locally. Liu et al., published on 15 May 2024, demonstrated entanglement between any pair of three independent atomic-memory nodes with maximum geographical separation 12.5 km. Craddock et al.'s preprint, first posted on 17 February 2026 and not peer reviewed, reports photonic entanglement swapping over 17.6 km of deployed New York City fiber, with CHSH Bell parameter S > 2 at measured swapping rates above 0.65 s⁻¹.
milestones.set_by: US Department of Energy, Quantum Internet Blueprint, milestone 2.

milestones.title: An intercity memory network stores entanglement and teleports qubits between any two users.
milestones.criterion: Between different cities, any two users obtain and store entangled qubits, teleport quantum information, and perform local measurements and operations. Memory storage meets the requirement imposed by round-trip classical communication time.
milestones.set_by: US Department of Energy, Quantum Internet Blueprint, milestone 3.
milestones.threshold_quote: INTERCITY QUANTUM COMMUNICATION USING ENTANGLEMENT SWAPPING.

not_found: Searches for intercity memory-network and continental cascaded-repeater demonstrations located no experimental report satisfying either complete DOE stage.
The full main text of the 2026 ion-memory paper and the supplied 2024 metropolitan-network PDF were inaccessible; their publisher abstracts were accessible.
Event counts underlying the cited ion-memory lifetime and teleportation-fidelity estimates were not located in the accessible texts.

results.finding: Entanglement between two nodes survived beyond its average establishment time over 10 km of spooled fibre.
results.detail: The provided abstract does not state the generation rate or decay time separately.
results.quote: Here we demonstrate memory–memory entanglement between two nodes connected by 10 km of spooled fibre surviving beyond the average entanglement establishment time.

results.finding: Two memory nodes generated entanglement at 0.83 Hz in the 107 μs storage experiment.
results.detail: The source reports storage beyond the round-trip communication time, but does not establish an entangled-state decoherence rate or η_link > 1.
results.quote:
The measured heralding probability is 6.9 × 10−4 and 8.0 × 10−4 for the first and second 
experiments, respectively, which corresponds to an entangling rate 
of 1.93 Hz and 0.83 Hz, considering the experiment repetition rate of 
2.76 kHz and 1.03 kHz.

results.finding: Any pair of three metropolitan memory nodes obtained entanglement, with maximum separation 12.5 km.
results.detail: A server heralded entanglement; the researchers verified it through local operations and measurements.
results.quote:
The memory nodes are maximally separated apart for 
12.5 kilometres. We actively stabilize the phase variance owing to fibre links and control 
lasers. We demonstrate concurrent entanglement generation between any two 
memory nodes.

results.finding: Two repeater segments were connected with 79.5 ± 4.8% entanglement fidelity, using 656 four-photon coincidences.
results.detail: Each segment’s entanglement-generation probability was set to 0.1%. The coincidences were collected over 16 hours; the output photons were post-selected.
results.quote:
The ﬁdelity of
the reconstructed state to the nearest maximally entangled state is
79.5(4.8)%.

results.finding: An atom-photon link retained 92.9 ± 2.8% entanglement fidelity after 1 ms; sample size was not stated.
results.detail: The second link was prepared with approximately 95% success within 1 ms at a 0.3% detection probability per trial. The source does not report the entanglement decay rate and generation rate needed to establish η_link > 1.
results.quote:
the atom-photon entan-
glement ﬁdelity in segment I changes only slightly in the1 ms
window, and remains as high as 92.9(2.8)% at 1 ms

results.finding: Entanglement swapping connected two links across a three-node diamond-spin network.
results.detail: A Bell-state measurement at the middle node established entanglement between the end nodes, with an estimated fidelity of 0.61.
results.quote:
The teleporter is prepared by establishing remote 
entanglement on the two links, followed by entanglement swapping on the middle 
node and storage in a memory qubit.

results.finding: Six cardinal qubit states were teleported between non-neighbouring nodes with average fidelity 0.702 ± 0.011.
results.detail: The conditional protocol achieved one teleportation per 117 s, following heralded preparation of the teleporter.
results.quote:
We find an average teleported state fidelity of 
F = 0.702(11) at an experimental rate of 1/(117 s).

results.finding: Two-source entanglement swapping yielded S > 2 over deployed fiber.
results.detail: A Bell-state measurement at the hub connected the two photonic links. The text does not report a total coincidence count.
results.quote:
We observe values
ofS >2 for measured swapping rates over 0.65 /s.

results.finding: Two spoke nodes shared swapped entanglement across 17.6 km of deployed fiber.
results.detail: The spokes were in separate rooms of the same building, connected through a remote hub. The experiment does not demonstrate entanglement between every pair of users in a multi-user network.
results.quote:
Additionally, we demonstrate the scalability of our method by maintaining the
quality of the entanglement swapping on 17.6 km of deployed fibers in NYC, relying on commercially
available SPADs at the spoke nodes, SNSPDs at the hub and standard time-synchronization tech-
niques.

results.finding: Trapped-ion repeater: 2,053 successful events; simulated feedforward yielded 72 ± 2% Bell-state fidelity.
results.detail: A deterministic Bell-state measurement connected two 25 km fiber links. The reported fidelity comes from a numerical feedforward calculation using the measured two-photon states.
results.quote: Observing one of the four logical states of the ion qubits heralds the projection of the polarisation of the remote telecom photons into one of four ideally orthogonal maximally-entangled states.

results.finding: Trapped-ion repeater connected two photon links, with 3,369 successes in 4,479,061 attempts.
results.detail: A deterministic Bell-state measurement on two ions swapped entanglement onto photons detected locally and after a 17 km deployed fiber. The reported 81.6% combined Bell-state fidelity assumes numerically simulated perfect feedforward.
results.quote: The repeater protocol was executed 67000 times over 4.5 hours, during which 4479061 attempts were made to establish photonic entanglement between nodes A and B, and 3369 successes occurred.

results.finding: A five-node relay demonstrated entanglement swapping over 40 km of fiber; the number of coincidence events was not reported.
results.detail: Two independent photon-pair sources were connected by a Bell-state measurement. The relay operated alongside classical traffic but did not include quantum memories.
results.quote: Entanglement swapping is demonstrated over a maximum fiber length of 40 km (four 10-km fibers) while simultaneously transmitting 10-Gbps classical data through all fibers.

results.finding: Two remote ion memory qubits stored entanglement for more than 100 times the state creation time.
results.detail: The fitted memory-entanglement decay time was 14 ± 4 s, versus an approximately 100 ms mean generation time, giving η_link ≈ 140. Storage used dynamical decoupling and sympathetic cooling.
results.quote:
We demonstrate storage of the remotely entangled memory qubits for ∼10 s, more than
100× the state creation time.

results.finding: A Bell-state measurement entangled two memories 14.5 km apart; sample size not reported.
results.detail: The measurement creates an elementary link by swapping photon-pair entanglement. Connecting separate elementary repeater links is proposed, not demonstrated.
results.quote:
A successful Bell-state measurement (BSM) at
node C heralds the entanglement, with outcomes time-
stamped and sent to nodes A and B.

results.finding: Two metropolitan quantum memories shared entanglement with 78.6 ± 2.0% fidelity; sample size not reported.
results.detail: The network has two memory-equipped end nodes and a central measurement node. Entanglement between arbitrary pairs in a multi-user network was not demonstrated.
results.quote:
This approach achieves heralded entan-
glement distribution between two solid-state quantum memories over a record 14.5 km separation,
generating a Bell state with a fidelity of78.6 ± 2.0%.

results.finding: Two atomic-ensemble memories were entangled over 420 km of fiber.
results.detail: Both memories were in the same laboratory, and much of the fiber was coiled. The experiment did not demonstrate intercity users or teleportation; the memories were read out 750 ns after atom-photon entanglement was created.
results.quote:
Here, we make a significant step further by reporting the
entanglement between two atomic ensemble quantum memories over 420 km.

results.finding: An elementary link between two qubits generated heralded entanglement at 0.022 s⁻¹.
results.detail: The qubits were protected while awaiting heralding signals, but the paper does not establish that the entanglement-generation rate exceeds the stored-entanglement decoherence rate.
results.quote:
The reduction in rate (0.022 s
−1
= 1.3 min
−1
at the predefined 15-ns window length) compared to the postselected case is mainly due to the added communication delay needed for the heralding signal to travel to the nodes, making each attempt a factor of ≈20 slower.

results.finding: Two metropolitan network nodes obtained heralded entanglement at a separation of 10 km.
results.detail: The nodes were in Delft and The Hague; the source demonstrates an intercity link rather than an intra-city network.
results.quote: Here, we report on heralded entanglement between two independently operated quantum network nodes separated by 10 kilometers.

results.finding: Two intercity qubit nodes received heralded entanglement with fidelity 0.534.
results.detail: The qubits were protected during heralding and locally measured, but the experiment did not demonstrate teleportation.

results.finding: A two-node atomic-memory link generated entanglement at 0.83 Hz.
results.detail: In this experiment, entanglement was stored for 107 μs. The source does not establish the stored-entanglement decay rate or demonstrate that the generation rate exceeds it.
results.quote: which corresponds to an entangling rate of 1.93 Hz and 0.83 Hz, considering the experiment repetition rate of 2.76 kHz and 1.03 kHz.

results.finding: All pairs of three atomic-memory nodes obtained entanglement in a metropolitan network spanning up to 12.5 km.
results.detail: The server switched between user pairs; entanglement was verified using local operations and measurements. The three links were served concurrently in time slots, not all in parallel.
results.quote: We demonstrated heralded entanglement generation between two quantum nodes situated 12.5 km apart, and the storage of entanglement exceeding the round-trip communication time. We also showed the concurrent entanglement generation on three links.

results.finding: A two-node diamond-spin link achieved a quantum link efficiency of approximately 8.
results.detail: The nodes were 2 metres apart. Entangled-state decoherence was suppressed using dynamical decoupling.
results.quote:
The combination of dynamical decoupling with the
single-photon entanglement protocol achieves a quantum
link eﬃciency ofη link∼ 8

results.finding: In a three-node network, entanglement swapping achieved an average Bell-state fidelity of 0.551 ± 0.013.
results.detail: The central node performed a Bell-state measurement on its two qubits, connecting the two previously established links.
results.quote:
Figure 5C compares the state ﬁdelities across the dif-
ferent BSM outcomes, displaying the expected lower ﬁ-
delities for outcomes of |1⟩ and an average ﬁdelity over
all outcomes of F = 0 .551(13).

results.finding: In a three-node network, the central memory qubit had an intrinsic dephasing time of 11.6 ± 0.2 ms.
results.detail: The paper also reports elementary-link generation rates, but does not establish that an elementary link's entanglement-generation rate exceeds its stored-entanglement decoherence rate.
results.quote:
We ﬁnd this intrinsic dephasing time to be
T∗2 = 11.6(2) ms, equivalent to the duration of≈ 2000 en-
tanglement generation attempts.

results.finding: A three-node network achieved any-to-any entanglement connectivity in two laboratories.
results.detail: The nodes were separated by meters within two laboratories; the demonstration was not an intra-city network.
results.quote:
We achieved multipar-
tite entanglement distribution across the three nodes and
any-to-any connectivity through entanglement swapping.
